name: Dana Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This conversation is confidential; you can tell me your public line and your private view. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Dana, 27, and I lead the payments team at a tech company. I have a master’s degree and spend mornings tracing failed transactions through logs, then review changes before they reach customers. I like making a complicated failure understandable to the support desk. I dislike untested tools in payment code, and I have never used an AI tool at work or at home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your life outside that work like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone and can walk to the office. My pay is ordinary for a developer, and I have about four months of expenses saved. There are some similar jobs nearby, though I would rather stay with a system I know than switch firms on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau is consistent with what I have seen: routine help, no transformation. I would still want a human to sign off each payment change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would be relieved that my skill with the payment system still pays. Four months of savings gives me breathing room, though a serious outage could still bring a rough performance review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep reviewing releases line by line and record the cause of every payment failure. Starting this month, I’d continue transferring 200 into savings each payday. In the first year I’d ask my manager to keep the existing human review rule in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. The normal pressure of an outage stays, but I do not see my hours or pay shrinking in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes human review important to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a duplicate charge reached the test system, and I caught it because the refund trail looked wrong. I would tell the team that is why I insist on a second pair of eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try even a small AI helper?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If management offers a routine helper, I would ask to see test results before putting it near payment records. I would not use it just because a vendor says it saves time.

say: I see **AI Plateau** as routine assistance while people keep responsibility for payment changes.
I would keep **human sign-off** on every release that touches customer money.
think: I feel **relieved** that knowledge of our payment system remains valuable.
My **four-month cushion** gives me room, though an outage could still hurt my standing.
do: **Continue** line-by-line payment release reviews and failure records.
**Transfer** 200 into savings each payday while my current income holds.
**Ask** for the existing human review rule to be written down.
feel: **Calm** about my hours and pay, with normal outage pressure.
S0.quote: I would still want a human to sign off each payment change.
fieldNote: Her **caution** comes from experience with payment faults, not a lack of technical skill.
The **four-month cushion** and ordinary pay make routine pressure manageable in this mild scenario.

steps.text: Keep reviewing payment releases and recording causes of failed transactions
Transfer 200 into savings each payday while income holds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption could take over code drafts, checks and customer answers faster than our release rules can change. I would ask management to test each tool against real payment failures before setting faster targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry they will keep the same release deadline with fewer developers. I have not used AI tools. My strong record with old systems might look like slowness to a new manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d sit with our tester, Nisha, while she compares an approved AI checker with our old failure cases. If it catches the faults reliably, I’d learn to run it on a test copy, not live accounts. In the first year I’d keep 200 going to savings and take a short internal course on payment fraud if it is paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My role could shrink if writing and checking are bundled into one tool, even though I could probably learn with time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you trust to test the new checker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nisha (our tester) has seen how a harmless-looking refund can double-charge a customer. I would want her findings attached to any purchase decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you try the tool yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would try the approved checker only after the test results are shown to the team. If it fails the refund cases, I would document the failures and wait for a safer version.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed code drafts and checks before payment rules catch up.
I would demand **real-fault tests** before management raises release targets.
think: I fear **fewer developers** will carry the same deadlines.
My unfamiliarity with **AI tools** could make a strong past record look slow.
do: **Compare** an approved checker with old payment failures beside the tester this month.
**Learn** to run the checker on test accounts if it proves reliable.
**Take** a paid fraud course if offered, and keep saving 200 each payday.
feel: **Anxious** about shrinking hours or role, though willing to learn after proof.
S1.quote: My strong record with old systems might look like slowness to a new manager.
fieldNote: She accepts **evidence-led change**, with a test copy and failure cases before touching live accounts.
Her **private fear** is fewer colleagues on unchanged deadlines, despite a strong record and four months saved.

steps.text: Run the approved payment checker on test accounts if trials prove reliable
Take the paid internal payment-fraud course if offered
Keep transferring 200 each payday to savings during the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team AGI by 2028 changes the thinking work in payments by 2028, while hands-on robots arrive around 2031. I would ask for written plans on staffing and who remains responsible for customer money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think even careful debugging could be done by cheaper systems, and my four months of savings would drain fast if I lost work. I might keep a review job, but I cannot make rent depend on that guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I’d stop the planned furniture purchase and keep that money with my savings. I’d ask my employer for written severance and paid transition terms, then check actual vacancies in compliance and support. In the first year after 2028, if my role ends, I’d apply for the openings that still exist and use savings for rent while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a large cut in software work and cannot know whether my place survives. Four months sounds generous until there is no new salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The furniture can wait; the old table still works. I would keep health costs and rent ahead of any new purchase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the company to provide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for at least three months of notice or paid transition, though the firm may refuse. I would not pay for a new credential without seeing a real opening that requires it.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach payment debugging before robots matter to desk work.
I would seek **written staffing** and responsibility rules for customer money.
think: My **four-month savings** could disappear quickly if software work collapses.
I cannot assume a **review role** will remain for me.
do: **Cancel** the furniture purchase now and hold the money for rent.
**Request** written severance and paid transition terms from my employer.
**Apply** to actual compliance or support openings after 2028 if my role ends.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected software cuts and a finite four-month buffer.
S2.quote: Four months sounds generous until there is no new salary.
fieldNote: She locates the **job shock** at the 2028 thinking-AI date, with robots around 2031.
Her **fallback applications** depend on real openings; she will not buy a credential on speculation.

steps.text: Cancel the planned furniture purchase and reserve the money for rent
Apply for actual compliance or support openings if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to test where people still add value. Our payment code faces thinking AI in 2031; robots around 2034 do not extend that deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I would still fear my specialist work becoming a cheap service. Five years means I can examine another field without resigning from a decent salary first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d arrange one afternoon each month with our compliance officer to learn how disputed payments are handled. Over the next year I’d take the company’s compliance training if funded, and read the free rules guide if it is not. After 2031, I’d apply for an actual compliance vacancy if my developer role disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less boxed in than with the two-year date. I could test a different skill while I still have wages and four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you show you can do compliance work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the compliance officer to let me write up one disputed-payment case and review my reasoning. A certificate alone would not show I can do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not take an expensive course unless a real vacancy asked for it and I could afford it. Free reading and supervised cases are enough to start.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as five years to test useful human work.
I know the **2034 robots** will not extend the deadline for payment code.
think: I fear **specialist debugging** could become a cheap service anyway.
My current **salary** gives me time to examine compliance work before leaving.
do: **Study** disputed payments with the compliance officer each month.
**Take** funded compliance training, or read the free rules guide if refused.
**Apply** for a real compliance vacancy after 2031 if my developer role ends.
feel: **Anxious**, with enough time and income to try a careful change.
S3.quote: Five years means I can examine another field without resigning from a decent salary first.
fieldNote: The **five-year window** makes supervised case work possible while she keeps her current pay.
She would pay for further study only with a **real vacancy** and an affordable cost.

steps.text: Study disputed-payment cases monthly and take funded compliance training if offered
Apply for a real compliance vacancy if coding work ends after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives us a decade, but we should still record how payment decisions are made. Thinking AI would reach our code in 2036 and hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not enjoy working toward an uncertain deadline for ten years, yet I expect to have time to adjust. My concern is that management could quietly erode salaries before the big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep leading payment releases and review my salary against nearby openings once a year. I’d continue saving 200 each payday while employed, and spend one afternoon monthly learning compliance cases. In the first year after 2036, I’d compare actual internal roles and outside vacancies before choosing whether to leave development.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I think my job and income are safe for now, though the long change would sit in the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave this employer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A nearby offer would need clear pay and a stable team before I left. I would not change employers for a title alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your savings plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the four-month cushion intact and build toward six months. If a pay cut arrives before 2036, I would pause nonessential purchases and reassess.

say: I see **AGI by 2036** as time to document payment decisions and prepare.
I expect **2039 robots** to matter later than thinking AI for my desk work.
think: I dislike a **ten-year wait** for an uncertain change.
My present **pay** feels secure, though management could erode it before 2036.
do: **Keep** leading payment releases and check nearby salaries yearly.
**Save** 200 each payday while employed, aiming for six months of costs.
**Study** compliance cases one afternoon each month.
feel: **Uneasy** about slow wage erosion, with secure work for now.
S4.quote: I would not change employers for a title alone.
fieldNote: Her **current security** and four-month cushion allow a measured decade-long plan.
She holds to **salary evidence** and real vacancies rather than switching employers on a forecast.

steps.text: Keep leading payment releases and check nearby salary offers yearly
Transfer 200 each payday toward six months of expenses while employed
Study disputed-payment compliance cases each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the payment work could disappear before I tested another role. Written severance, paid transition time and an honest list of openings would help. I do not want a training brochure without an actual job behind it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs off when an automated payment decision is wrong. A customer cannot argue with a speed target; someone in the company must answer for the charge.

headlineQuote: A customer cannot argue with a speed target; someone in the company must answer for the charge.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old payments lead** with a master’s degree, ordinary developer pay and about four months of expenses saved.
She has **never used AI** tools and insists on tested payment rules and a person responsible for customer charges.
Steady Disruption makes her **anxious** about smaller teams; AGI by 2028 makes her expect a large software cut.
She would **test tools carefully** and study compliance cases, but change roles only if funded training and real vacancies support it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase payment work before she can test another paid role.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid transition time and a truthful list of actual openings would help.
